description: Baseline prediction of historical trends in ASEAN energy systems without policy impacts.
pathwayDescription:
The ASEAN Centre for Energy (ACE) acts as the ASEAN energy data center and knowledge hub and produces the ACE ASEAN Energy Outlook providing energy pathways for Southeast Asia. The ACE Baseline scenario (BAS) is a predictive pathway that extrapolates observed historic trends of the ASEAN Member States (AMS) energy systems into the future. It assumes a business-as-usual level of effort and specifically disregards modelling any policy interventions, even existing ones to meet national energy efficiency (EE) and renewable energy (RE) targets. Hence, it also excludes firm plant capacity additions based on power development plans (PDP). The extrapolation of past trends also implies that technology costs remain static and new technologies do not benefit from learning rates.

As a conservative baseline pathway, ACE BAS forecasts emissions at the ASEAN level to more than double by 2050.

coreDrivers.investmentChange: Average annual Power investment rises from USD 20.0bn in 2023–2030 to USD 27.7bn in 2041–2050, driven by a high share of fossil fuel investments.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Population and GDP growth are a common underlying demand driver across all ACE scenarios and extracted from World Bank and ADB projections.

dependencies.dependency_description: No additional policy strategy is required or modelled. BAS is the no-intervention reference pathway.
Stable electrification rates limit on adoption of new end-use technologies.
Existing grids and infrastructure support the historical trajectory of the power sector. Energy storage and regional grid optimisation are not central levers in the BAS pathway.

Availability of fuels for power generation and trade are bounded by proven reserves and existing renewable potential, with no assumed new exploration. Fossil fuel reliance means that ASEAN becomes a net importer of natural gas in 2027, while exporting coal until 2050. No hard limitation for scaling up power generation in BAS though.
BAS produces the smallest fossil-sector job losses, so workforce disruption is limited relative to the other pathways. But it also creates the least amount of new jobs in renewable energy.
